newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: World oilseeds output to dip, consumption to rise.
newsitem.headline: World oilseeds output to dip, consumption to rise.

text.p: World production of oilseeds will dip slightly in the 1996/97 season to about 255 million tonnes against 257 million tonnes in 1995/96, an official of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) said on Wednesday.

"Global production of the seven major oilseeds is forecast at 255 million tonnes," Micaela Maftei, an official of the intergovernmental group on Oilseeds, Oils and Fats with the FAO, said at an Asian Oilseeds conference in Singapore.

"The combination of sharply reduced carry-over stocks in all regions, except for parts of Africa and Latin America, with only moderate increases in oilseed production, points to a continued tightness of oilseed supplies in 1996/97," Maftei said.
But the FAO official said global demand for oils and fats "is still expected to rise, largely on account of further increases in demand in Asia."
"The bulk of world import requirements of oils should be met by palm oil from Indonesia and Malaysia," the official added.
Soybean exports will still be dominated by the United States despite inroads into the market made by Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay.
"China also exported significant quantities of soybeans, but the availabilities are expected to decrease sharply in the future as a result of growing domestic demand of oils and meals," Maftei said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has estimated the U.S. would cover about 63 percent of the world trade in soybeans, which is estimated to reach 34.4 million tonnes by the year 2002.
Growth in consumption of oils and fats is strongest in Asia, with average per capita consumption nearly doubling in the last 15 years to 11.0 kg in 1995 from 6.5 kg.
In China alone, consumption surged to 9.4 kg 1995 from 3.8 kg in 1980. The rate of consumption in Thailand is expanding by 8.0 percent per annum and 6.1 percent annually for Malaysia.
In Europe, consumption is growing by only 1.4 percent and 1.2 percent in North and Central America.
The leading sources of oilseeds, oils and fats would still be soybeans and palm oil.
Malaysia and Indonesia will continue to be the main exporters of palm oil.

"Indonesia enjoys a competitive advantage in producing palm over Malaysia and the country's share in the total palm oil exports is expected to continue to grow at the expense of Malaysia," the FAO official said.

He said the Philippines is also expected to maintain its dominance in exports of coconut oil, but supplies will continue to fluctuate widely because of cyclical variations in output and weather disturbances which may hit the country.
